title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: Money and Mud—The World of Our Mutual Friend

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, a podcast dedicated to one of the greatest, strangest, and most underrated novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and over the coming episodes we'll be working through Charles Dickens's last completed novel — Our Mutual Friend — chapter by chapter, passage by passage.
It's a novel about money — who has it, who craves it, who is destroyed by it — and about what human beings are worth when you strip away the price tag.
Three brilliant guests join me today, and I want to introduce them properly because each brings something genuinely different to the table.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative-writing teacher who thinks about how fiction is built — the architecture of sentences, the machinery of images.
She has a rare ability to make technical craft feel thrilling, and Dickens gives her a great deal to work with.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who specialises in the institutions that literature depicts — the workhouses, the courts, the charitable missions.
He brings the documentary evidence — what Dickens's world actually was — and he is not afraid to get angry about it.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has returned to it many times since.
She's our guide to the reading experience itself — what moves you, what makes you laugh, what makes you stop and re-read a sentence in quiet astonishment.
Today's opening segment asks the foundational question: what kind of world is this novel?
Money and mud — those are its twin elements.
James, you've been thinking about Dickens's social satire — and there is a passage early in the novel that I think is one of the most brilliantly cruel comic inventions in all of Victorian fiction.
The Twemlow passage, yes — and it's worth pausing on the sheer audacity of what Dickens does there.
He introduces a human being — a gentleman, a man of blood and standing — as, and I quote directly, an innocent piece of dinner-furniture.
"There was an innocent piece of dinner-furniture that went upon easy castors and was kept over a livery stable-yard in Duke Street, Saint James's, when not in use."
That single sentence does an enormous amount of ideological work.
Twemlow is not a person to the Veneerings — he is a mechanism, stored away when not required, retrieved when a dinner table needs expanding.
And the joke deepens when Dickens spells out the logic: the further Twemlow was pulled out — the more guests added — the further he drifted from the centre and toward the sideboard.
Social utility and social marginality are, in this world, the same thing.
What strikes me structurally is that Dickens doesn't just use the furniture metaphor once and move on — he extends it systematically, leaf by leaf.
Sometimes Twemlow and half a dozen leaves, sometimes a dozen leaves, sometimes pulled out to his utmost extent of twenty leaves.
That repetition — the accumulation of numbers — mimics the very social inflation it's describing.
The prose enacts what it satirises.
And the best quote is the one James mentioned — the line about being in frequent requisition and representing the dining-table in its normal state.
"Being first cousin to Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state."
The normal state of a table is absence — it exists to be used, not to exist in itself.
Dickens has compressed an entire theory of how the Victorian aristocracy was instrumentalised by the newly rich into a single clause.
And I think what makes it so delicious to read is that Twemlow himself remains perfectly, blissfully unaware of the metaphor being applied to him.
He is described as a source of blind confusion to the Veneerings — not the other way round.
The comedy lives entirely in the gap between his self-understanding and his social function.
But I also want to say — Twemlow is one of the few people in the Veneering world who has actual goodness in him.
Dickens is gentle with him, even while being savage about the system that uses him.
That's an important distinction — the satire in this novel is almost never about individuals being wicked.
It's about systems — social, financial, institutional — that corrupt or diminish perfectly ordinary people.
Which brings me to a passage I find genuinely harrowing — the moment John Harmon reads his own death notice.
This is the Gothic, horrifying underside of everything the Veneering dinner-party scenes float above.
John Harmon — the man whose inherited fortune drives the entire plot — recounts finding a crowd gathered around a placard announcing his own murder.

"I perceived that Radfoot had been murdered by some unknown hands for the money for which he would have murdered me, and that probably we had both been shot into the river from the same dark place into the same dark tide."
The repetition — same dark place, same dark tide — is Dickens at his most controlled.
Money sets these men on identical trajectories toward the same violent end.
That passage unlocks something about how the novel is structured at a much larger level.
The river is not incidental — it is the novel's central nervous system.
Everything that the polished society world above pretends isn't there — death, greed, bodies — gets literalised in that water.
Harmon's identity dissolves in it; Radfoot's corpse is pulled from it; the Hexam family live off what it yields.
The horror of 'in a wild incautious way I hurried there' — Harmon going to view what he believes to be himself — that's almost unbearable.
And yet — and this is what makes Dickens extraordinary — the same novel that contains that Gothic horror also contains Mr. Wilfer's blessing on Bella's engagement.
It's one of the most purely tender moments in the novel, and it turns the whole money theme on its head.
He calls Bella a mercenary young person — ironically, lovingly — because she has done the opposite of what everyone expected.

"I love this young person dearly. I say to the man of this young person's heart, out of my heart and with all of it, 'My blessing on this engagement betwixt you, and she brings you a good fortune when she brings you the poverty she has accepted for your sake and the honest truth's!'"
Poverty as fortune.
That's the moral inversion the entire novel has been building toward.
Wilfer is a wonderful figure precisely because his goodness is entirely undignified.
He has no money, no social leverage, no institutional power of any kind.
And yet his moral authority in that scene is absolute.
There is a related moment with the Milveys that I think belongs in this conversation — it's played as comedy, but it encodes something similar.
Mrs Sprodgkin — a magnificently tedious parishioner — has to be bribed with tea, sugar, bread, and butter before the Milveys can leave for the station.
And Dickens notes, with perfect deadpan, that she regarded the gifts in a rather elevated light —
"she regarded tea and sugar in the light of myrrh and frankincense, and considered bread and butter identical with locusts and wild honey."
It's absurd, yes — but Dickens's real target is not Mrs Sprodgkin.
It's the institutional church's failure to do anything useful — and the extraordinary patience required of the few people who actually try.
So we have, within a few passages, a man reduced to furniture, a corpse in a river, a father calling poverty a fortune, and a woman receiving bread and butter as sacred offering.
That is the range of this novel.
In the next segment, we'll turn to the characters at the heart of it — the people this world shapes, destroys, and occasionally redeems.

segments.title: The Architecture of Reinvention: How Dickens Builds Harmon's Secret

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart, passage by passage, to see how it works and why it still matters.
I'm your host, and today we're diving into one of the most architecturally ambitious things Dickens ever attempted: the slow, deliberate construction of John Harmon's secret identity.
With me today are three readers who bring very different lenses to this extraordinary novel.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose passion is the architecture of fiction — the structural choices that make a book cohere or collapse.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who specializes in the institutions that Victorian fiction both depicts and distorts.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has been reading and re-reading this novel since her teens, and who has very strong feelings about which characters deserve better.
Welcome, all three of you.
Let's begin with the audacity of what Dickens is doing here — he is asking readers to hold a secret in plain sight for hundreds of pages.
Eleanor, I want to start with you: how does Dickens himself account for this strategy?
What's remarkable is that Dickens steps out from behind the curtain entirely — which he almost never does — and addresses the reader directly about his own method.
He actually names what he was doing and what he expected certain readers to get wrong.
Here's the passage — and it's one of the most fascinating authorial intrusions in all of Victorian fiction:

"I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he."
He's drawing a distinction between concealment and suggestion — and that distinction is the whole game.
The mystery isn't hidden; it's lit from the side, so that readers who look straight at it see shadow, and readers who look sideways see the shape.
That's an incredibly sophisticated structural choice — and then he has the confidence to explain it to us afterward, trusting that explanation won't diminish the achievement.
There's something a little combative about that passage too, I think.
He says he was not alarmed by the anticipation — which is Dickens being polite about the fact that he found a certain kind of reader mildly insufferable.

The phrase he uses — 'thinking it worth while, in the interests of art, to hint to an audience that an artist may perhaps be trusted to know what he is about' — that is a rebuke dressed as a courtesy.
And the social context matters here: serialized fiction was consumed by an enormously varied readership, many of whom wrote directly to Dickens while the novel was in progress.
The pressure to be legible — to be immediately, unambiguously clear — was real and commercial.
So his insistence on artistic patience in the face of that pressure is not a small thing.
And as a reader, I can tell you that the strategy works — it worked when I first read the novel at sixteen, and it still works now.
You do sense something — there's an unease around Rokesmith that you can't quite name.
But what Dickens layers underneath the identity plot is all this emotional backstory — the Boffins' relationship with the boy John Harmon — and that, for me, is what gives the secret its weight.
The Boffins aren't just convenient guardians of the secret — they genuinely loved the boy.
And Boffin tells Lightwood about it in this extraordinary, almost bumbling, but deeply tender testimony.
Yes — and that Boffin testimony is one of the passages I most wanted to discuss today.
James, will you take us into it?
This passage is doing a lot of legal and social work, even as it sounds like a man fumbling for words at a kitchen table.
Boffin is establishing, for Lightwood — who is effectively the family's solicitor — that he and Mrs Boffin consistently acted in John's interest against the old man's cruelty.
It's testimony, as Caroline said — it has the rhetorical shape of sworn evidence, even in Boffin's vernacular.
And then comes the moment that's really quite startling in its physicality:

"I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet — she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head — and send it spinning across the yard."
And then — and this is the sentence that lands like a fist:
"Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her."
The repetition of 'dropped her' is Dickens at his most purely theatrical — two words, a full stop, two words again.
It records the violence and refuses to soften it with a single syllable of explanation.
That sentence is a masterclass in rhythm as meaning.
The bonnet detail — the black straw, perched as a matter of convenience — is pure Dickens comedy, and then the violence arrives and obliterates the comedy in a single clause.
It's the same structural move he uses across the whole Harmon plot: charm and warmth building trust, then the darkness arriving without warning.
What I find equally remarkable is what this passage does for our understanding of Mrs Boffin — she becomes, here, genuinely heroic.
She absorbed a blow meant for the boy.
And that act of protection seeds everything that comes later — her desire to adopt a child and name him John Harmon, to keep the boy alive in some form.
That connection is so important — and the adoption proposal is one of the passages I find most quietly devastating in the novel.
Mrs Boffin says it almost apologetically — 'say it's only a whim' — as if she's embarrassed by the depth of her own feeling.
But listen to what she actually proposes:
"Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him."
She wants to make the money mean something — to redirect it through love rather than let it sit as a monument to injustice.
And there's a gothic undertone, isn't there — name a living child after a dead one, summon the lost boy back through an act of charity.
The irony, of course, is that John Harmon is alive — but she doesn't know that yet.
And that dramatic irony is structurally load-bearing throughout the novel.
The reader — or at least the reader paying attention, as Dickens pointedly suggests — holds information that most of the characters do not.
Which brings me to the question of what Harmon himself is doing during this long disguise — and whether Dickens gives him adequate self-knowledge.
Because there's another character in this novel whose self-knowledge is handled very differently — Eugene Wrayburn — and I think the contrast is instructive.
Oh, the Wrayburn self-knowledge passage — yes, I've been waiting to get to that.
Lightwood tries to push him toward thinking about the future, and Eugene cuts him off with what amounts to a clinical diagnosis of his own character.
Dickens writes that Eugene says it 'with a perplexed and inquisitive face, as if he actually did not know what to make of himself.'
And then Lightwood begins — 'Look on to the end—' — and Eugene catches the words and responds:
"That's exactly what I am incapable of doing."
Five words — and they contain an entire character study.
The gap between self-knowledge and self-correction is Eugene's tragedy — and Harmon's disguise, in contrast, is a form of elaborate self-correction without any visible self-knowledge at all.
That distinction matters enormously to the reading experience.
Eugene is the character I believe in more completely — because his self-knowledge is also self-entrapment, and you feel that every time he speaks.
Harmon's disguise, by contrast, keeps him slightly opaque to the reader — you're watching from the outside even when you're supposedly inside his confidence.
And yet the moment the secret breaks open — the moment Bella understands what's been happening — the emotion is completely real.
Which brings us to that revelation scene — Bella kneeling beside Mr Boffin and retracting everything she thought she knew.
Caroline, you've described it as emotionally real — but it's also structurally very unusual, isn't it?
It is — because Dickens chooses to give Bella the discovery not through argument or logic but through a kind of bodily intuition.
She deposits the baby in John's arms — this little domestic act of trust — and then she simply kneels beside Boffin and speaks.
And what she says is formally the most jubilant thing in the novel:
"Please I have found out something not yet mentioned. Please I don't believe you are a hard-hearted miser at all, and please I don't believe you ever for one single minute were!"
The triple 'please' — it's the grammar of a child addressing a beloved elder, reclaiming the relationship from its distorted form.
She's not apologising — she's celebrating.
The comedy and the tenderness work together there in a way that's technically very hard to achieve.

Dickens writes that she cried it 'with an exultant ringing laugh as she struggled with him and forced him to turn his delighted face to hers' — that physical detail of struggling to make him look at her is perfect.
It's slapstick in service of revelation — and the whole Harmon plot has been building toward exactly this kind of earned, unembarrassed feeling.
What the architecture achieves is that we trust Bella's transformation because we've watched it happen under pressure — real pressure, not confected sentiment.
The word 'architecture' keeps coming up, and rightly so — because Dickens is doing something that the serialized form makes almost impossibly difficult.
He's asking readers to carry a suspended question — is Harmon alive? — across months of publication, without ever allowing the tension to go slack.
And he threads the novel's other great images through that tension — including one of the most striking in the book, the train crossing the river.
Eleanor, you wanted to bring in that passage — it strikes me as a kind of structural metaphor for everything we've been discussing.
It really is — and it's one of those passages that seems at first like pure descriptive set piece and then reveals itself as something much more purposeful.
Listen to this:

"The train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river: bursting over the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded in the rush of smoke and steam and glare."
And then — just as you think the image is complete — Dickens extends it into something philosophical:
"going straight to its end, as Father Time goes to his."
The train becomes time itself — indifferent, unstoppable, crossing the river that has already claimed one body and may claim more.
It's Dickens embedding mortality into a piece of Victorian infrastructure — the newest technology in the world made to carry the oldest theme.
What moves me about that passage is the phrase 'the quiet surface' — because the river is so rarely quiet in this novel.
It's a working river — a dredging river, a death-dealing river — and for one moment the train's violence makes it seem still by comparison.
And the secrecy of Harmon's identity is bound up in that river — he was supposed to have drowned in it.
The river keeps the secret.
'The river keeps the secret' — that's a phrase worth sitting with.
What strikes me, pulling together everything we've discussed today, is how much Dickens trusts his reader — and how deliberately he earns that trust back.

The Boffins' love for the boy establishes the emotional stakes, the disguise tests every character who encounters Rokesmith, and the revelation, when it comes, is proportionate to everything that preceded it.
Eleanor, James, Caroline — this has been a genuinely wonderful conversation.
Next time, we'll be turning to the dust mounds themselves — what they meant to Victorian readers, and what they mean now.
Until then — thank you for listening to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.

segments.title: Reading for Laughter: The Comic Genius of Dickens's Peripheral Souls

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've spent time with the novel's great tragic and romantic arcs — but today we're turning to something equally essential: the comedy.
Dickens peoples the margins of his story with figures of extraordinary comic invention — and in Our Mutual Friend, none more so than Silas Wegg.
Caroline Woodcourt has been living with these passages, and I think she's been enjoying herself rather a lot.
Caroline — where do we start?
We start with a man falling over.
That is almost always the right place to start with Dickens.
In this passage, Wegg is reading aloud to his partner-in-crime Mr Venus — reading about hidden wills, hidden money — and he is getting more and more excited.
Dickens tracks this excitement through Wegg's wooden leg, which gradually elevates of its own accord as the greed mounts.
And then the wonderful sentence arrives, describing the moment both men simply stop functioning.
"Both remaining in a kind of pecuniary swoon."
A pecuniary swoon.
The word "pecuniary" is doing extraordinary work there — it's so formal, so clinical, placed next to "swoon," which is pure swooning romance.
That collision of registers is exactly what makes Dickens's comic prose so technically interesting.
He reaches for the language of high sentiment — swooning, rapture — and applies it to money, which is the most debased of motives.
The joke is conceptual before it's even verbal.
And I love the physical specificity leading into it — the wooden leg gradually elevating, the elbow nudging deeper and deeper.
Dickens maps greed onto the body with absolute precision.
The wooden leg isn't just a comic prop — it becomes a barometer of moral temperature.
What strikes me, coming at this from a different angle, is how accurate the scheme actually is.
In the next passage, Wegg lays out his extortion plan with a kind of demented legal thoroughness.
He describes what he calls a "conditional clause" — and the conditional clause is, essentially, blackmail with graduated pricing.
Listen to the language Dickens gives him — it mimics the syntax of a legal instrument almost perfectly.
"He considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, 'Halves!'"
"Stateable" — he's invented a legal-sounding word to give his greed the dignity of a contract.
And then it escalates — Halves might not be enough, it might be Two-thirds, it might be Three-fourths — and he invites correction from his partner on this point.
The satirical point is very sharp: this is how actual sharp practice dressed itself up, in the language of reasonableness.
And then there's the phrase that stops me every time — the phrase about what will happen to Boffin if he misbehaves.
"He should be kept in a state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom."
"Abject moral bondage and slavery" — coming from Silas Wegg.
The man is a literary ballad-vendor with a wooden leg who has been eating a stewed mutton chop and telling himself he's a mastermind.
The gap between the rhetoric and the reality is so enormous it becomes its own comic engine.
That gap is the engine, yes — and Dickens sustains it through a very specific technical choice: he never lets Wegg's voice drop.
We get this wonderful scene later where Wegg comes to the keyhole of Boffin's house and performs this extraordinary wordless act of menace.
It's almost entirely physical — and yet it's among the funniest things in the novel.
"Silas made no reply, but laboured with a will at turning an imaginary grindstone outside the keyhole, while Mr Boffin stooped at it within; he then laughed silently, and stumped home."
"Laughed silently."
Two words that are somehow both sinister and absurd at once — the laugh is real, but we can't hear it, and Boffin can't either.
It's pure theatrical mime, and it reveals how much of Dickens's comedy is rooted in the body expressing what language cannot.
The grindstone is such a layered image.
Grinding someone down — keeping someone's nose to the grindstone — these were live metaphors for the coercive employment relationship.
Wegg is miming an act of economic domination — he genuinely believes he's the master now.
And yet the imaginary grindstone is so visually preposterous that the power is entirely deflated before it begins.
Dickens is doing something characteristic here: he lets his villains feel enormous — and then the world reduces them.
And when the reduction comes — when the world actually catches up with Wegg — it comes fast, and physically.
There's a passage near the end where Wegg is mid-sneer, mid-sarcastic-retort, when Harmon simply grabs him.
"He found himself gripped by the cravat; shaken until his teeth chattered; shoved back, staggering, into a corner of the room; and pinned there."
The semicolons are doing so much work in that sentence — each one is another physical blow, landing in sequence.
We've watched Wegg plot and posture for hundreds of pages — and Dickens dispatches him in one syntactically ruthless sentence.
There's a real satisfaction to it — but also something comic in the sheer speed.
That compression is a structural choice as much as a comic one.
Dickens has been building Wegg's self-importance through rhetorical excess — all those rolling "That, he would beg to remind" constructions.
And then he answers that verbal inflation with pure physical economy.
It's the same structural instinct you see in the John Harmon passage — all that elaborate triple identity, the oakum hair stowed in a coat — handled with such casual speed.
Dickens is always working with the gap between how large things feel and how quickly they can be disposed of.
The Harmon passage is a strange one to end on — it's comic but it's also genuinely unsettling.
One man, three names — and Dickens tells us plainly that each name is as fully that person as any other.
"John Rokesmith, too, was as like that same lost wanted Mr Julius Handford as never man was like another in this world."
The repetition of that phrase — "as never man was like another" — makes it feel like a legal definition, or perhaps a philosophical paradox.
Identity in this novel is always something you can stow in a coat pocket, apparently.
That image of identity stowed in a coat pocket might be the most compressed summary of Our Mutual Friend's concerns I've heard.
The comedy is never just decoration here — it carries the novel's deepest preoccupations about who people are and how much that can be changed.
Caroline, Eleanor, James — thank you.
We'll be back shortly to follow the money further — and to ask what Dickens is really saying about what it does to people.

segments.title: Gold Dust and Moral Corruption: Boffin's Fall and Dickens's Critique of Wealth

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast where we take one of the great Victorian novels apart — carefully — to see what's inside.
Today we're turning to one of the novel's most urgent preoccupations: wealth, and what it does to people.
The Boffin fortune — built on dust heaps — sits at the moral centre of Our Mutual Friend, and Dickens uses it to expose the ugliness that money attracts.
With me today are three exceptional readers of this novel.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose eye for how Dickens constructs his effects is, frankly, unmatched.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who will keep us honest about what the world of this novel actually looked like from the outside.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and can find the music in a sentence others might miss.
Let's begin with the flood — the extraordinary satirical catalogue of begging letters that descends on Boffin the moment his inheritance becomes public.
What strikes me immediately about these passages is that Dickens doesn't give us Boffin reading the letters — he gives us the Secretary reading them.
That's a significant structural choice, and it creates a very particular irony.
The man of new wealth is insulated from the spectacle of greed by his employee — and yet the spectacle is still there, vast and comic and grotesque.
Dickens opens with a wonderful rhetorical question — he asks what set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety.
And then he reels off the list: fifty-seven churches, forty-two parsonage houses, seven-and-twenty organs.
The accumulation is the joke — and the critique.
Every institution, every petitioner, sees Boffin not as a person but as a source — as gold dust to be harvested.
Eleanor's point about the Secretary as filter is well taken — and historically, that's exactly right.
A man of Boffin's sudden wealth in the 1860s would have been deluged — there's no other word for it — by exactly this kind of appeal.
The charitable sector was vast, chaotically organised, and heavily dependent on what we might call social leverage — getting aristocratic names onto letterheads.
Which brings us to the Duke of Linseed's letter — and this is where Dickens is doing something precise and rather brilliant.
"Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet."
That description is doing the satirical work before the letter even opens.
Fat, double, sealed — everything about it performing importance, prestige, intimacy.
And then comes the postscript: the Steward's fee is limited to three guineas.
Dickens notes the letter is only lithographed by the hundred — the ducal intimacy is mass-produced.
I want to go to the individual beggars, because that passage is where my heart genuinely breaks — and then immediately mends from laughter.
Dickens is doing something almost impossible there — holding comedy and tragedy in the same breath.
The daughters of general officers — long accustomed to every luxury of life, he says, except spelling.
That parenthesis — "except spelling" — is so small, so cruel, and so perfectly placed.
But the line I keep returning to is the one about their documents — let me find it.
"They call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf."
Minced veal to a calf — that simile is so unexpected, so earthy, and somehow so right.
The pathos of people clutching scraps they call documents — it is devastating, even inside the comedy.
And that tonal double-bind is, I think, precisely Dickens's argument about what money does.
It reduces everyone around it — the petitioners become comic, the wealthy become targets, the whole social transaction becomes grotesque.
The beggars on horseback, needing a clock or a violin or an astronomical telescope — the specificity of that list is extraordinary.
Dickens makes the requests precise enough to be almost plausible — which makes them funnier and more pitiable at the same time.
The beggars of punctual business-habits who will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday — that's blackmail dressed as tragedy.
There's a larger structural irony at work here that I think Dickens is quite deliberate about.
The wealth that attracts all this desperate, comic, predatory attention — John Harmon himself arrived in England already shrinking from it.
Harmon's own account of his return is worth sitting with for a moment.
"I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife."
The repetition of shrinking — twice — is so telling.
He also confesses to being mistrustful of himself — growing avaricious, he fears, as though wealth were a contagion he'd already been exposed to.
So we have Boffin receiving the money, Harmon fleeing from it — and both men are defined by their relationship to a fortune built on literal refuse.
That phrase — mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife — is so sad, isn't it.
Because of course Bella Wilfer is the woman he's been designated to marry — and at this point in the story, she is, quite honestly, mercenary.
Harmon's fear is not paranoid — it's accurate.
And yet the novel also insists that people can change — that Bella is capable of moral growth.
What moves me is that Harmon says he knows of nothing but wretchedness that his father's wealth had ever brought about.
The dust heap inheritance is not a fairy-tale gift — it's a curse that everyone in the novel is trying to negotiate their relationship with.
Which is what makes the Wegg subplot so perfectly positioned as a dark mirror.
Wegg's great discovery — the will he believes will overturn everything — reduces John Harmon senior to his most naked sentiment about his own family.
Wegg reads it out with that extraordinary oily relish.

"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown."
That will is a portrait of a man made miserly and bitter by his own wealth — he dies having made no friends, having broken his family.
And the phrase quite enough for him — directed at Boffin — is such a sneer from beyond the grave.
The legal instrument of the will is a beautiful vehicle for Dickens here, because wills are public statements of private feeling.
In the real Victorian world, a will could and frequently did encode spite, control, disinheritance — it was a legal document with a moral argument inside it.
Old Harmon uses his will to punish and posthumously condescend — and Boffin's entire story proceeds from that act.
And what Wegg and Venus think they have found is leverage — a way to weaponise the old man's second thoughts.
But the irony is that their scheme is just another form of the begging letters — another predator circling the gold dust.
And meanwhile Fledgeby is doing the same thing, only with better manners and worse morals.
That scene with Lammle where he accuses him of treating him like a doll and puppet — it's Fledgeby at his most revealing.
He says: "don't you on that account come talking to me as if I was your doll and puppet, because I am not."
The defensive vanity there is so perfectly captured — he knows he showed to no advantage, he says so openly, but he refuses to accept subordination.
Everyone in this novel is trying to establish their position relative to money and power — and Fledgeby, for all his nastiness, is at least honest about the game.
That's the thing — Dickens keeps showing us that the corrupting force of wealth is not confined to the poor or the villainous.
It reaches from the Duke of Linseed's lithographed intimacy to Fledgeby's meanest of eyes to Wegg's blandly buoyant blackmail.
Every social register is implicated — the aristocrat, the schemer, the desperate, the fraudulent philanthropist.
The gold dust doesn't make its neighbours golden — it makes them grasping.
That image — gold dust making its neighbours grasping rather than golden — feels like an almost perfect summary of what Dickens is doing in this novel.
We've ranged from the satirical extravagance of those begging letters to the genuine tragedy inside John Harmon's confession, to the cold mechanics of Wegg's schemes.
In our next segment, we'll turn to what the novel imagines as a possible escape from all this — the question of whether goodness, genuine goodness, can survive the dust heap.

segments.title: The Woman Remade: Bella's Arc from Mercenary to Human

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — as seriously as it deserves.
Today we're diving into one of the novel's most contested achievements: the transformation of Bella Wilfer.
She begins the novel as self-described mercenary — sharp-tongued, money-hungry, entirely lovable in her honesty about it.
By the end, she has become something richer and more complicated — and we want to know exactly how Dickens pulls that off.
With me today are three people whose different lenses on the novel I find endlessly illuminating.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a literary critic and novelist who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — with genuine awe at how the parts fit.
Professor James Blackstone brings the social historian's eye — what the world of this novel actually felt like from the inside, legally and economically.
And Ms Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since adolescence and reads it with the kind of intimacy that only long love produces.
Let's begin with the machinery behind Bella's arc — the plot device Dickens uses to put her transformation in motion.
What strikes me first about Bella's arc is that Dickens buries the mechanism quite deep in the novel's architecture.
John Harmon's confession — the passage where he explains exactly why he remained dead — is essential for understanding what's really happening to Bella.
He tells us, in that long soliloquy, that the plot grew out of a very specific uneasiness — a desire to see his allotted wife before she could possibly know him for himself.
And then he spells out the scheme:
'the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way.'
That word 'throwing' is wonderfully physical — they are hurling themselves into her orbit, as if Bella were a gravitational force to be tested.
And the test is not of her beauty or her manners — it's of her character under conditions she cannot curate.
That scheme has a legal and social dimension that is easy to miss if you're reading for the romance.
Harmon's father has effectively sold his son in the will — Bella is property to be inherited along with the dust-heap fortune.
John Harmon understands this with a kind of moral revulsion that Dickens renders with unusual precision.
He says his motive is:
'The dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that seemed to have fallen on my father's riches — the fate that they should lead to nothing but evil.'
'Nothing but evil' — that is not a reformer's pamphlet phrase; that is a man who has grown up inside that money and felt its corrupting weight on everything around him.
The dust-heap fortune, in Dickens's moral economy, is original sin made literal — and Bella is the intended inheritor of its guilt.
Harmon's disguise is therefore not a romantic trick — it is a quarantine measure.
James's word 'quarantine' is exactly right, and it also captures something of how the novel feels — sealed off, pressurised.
But what I want to say about Bella is that she is never passive in this arrangement, even when she doesn't know the arrangement exists.
The transformation Dickens traces is genuinely hers — not something done to her by Harmon's scheme, but something she enacts.
And what's interesting to me is how Dickens shows us other women in the novel who are also remaking themselves — or being remade by circumstance.
That rooftop scene with Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren — it's doing something very similar, though in a completely different register.
Dickens gives us this extraordinary image:
'they both pored over one book; both with attentive faces; Jenny with the sharper; Lizzie with the more perplexed.'
Two women learning, side by side, above the city that has used them both — it's genuinely moving.
Caroline has put her finger on something important — the rooftop is a pastoral space in the middle of industrial London.
Dickens surrounds Lizzie and Jenny with chimneys that he personifies with this magnificent, faintly absurd comedy.
The chimneys are 'bridling, and fanning themselves, and looking on in a state of airy surprise' — they are scandalized dowagers at a garden party.
That comic framing is doing serious work: it makes the scene safe, warm, almost fairy-tale — and then the learning happening inside it hits harder.
Self-improvement, in this novel, is never merely personal — it is always a kind of defiance.
Bella defies the fate the will assigned her; Lizzie defies what the river and her father's life marked her out to be.
And both arcs are shadowed, quite literally, by death.
This is a novel in which the river keeps offering up bodies, and the first body is Gaffer Hexam — Lizzie's own father.
Riderhood's cry when he sees the recovered corpse is almost operatic in its brevity:
'Gaffer's done me. It's Gaffer!'
Three words, then three words — and the world contracts to a single recognition.
The irony is colossal: the man who made his living from other people's dead now is the found dead — his accuser becomes his mourner in the same breath.
Lizzie carries that weight — her father's trade, his death, the river's appetite — through every chapter of her own transformation.
What strikes me about the novel's violence is that Dickens always wraps it in landscape — and the landscape is always morally loaded.
That passage where Bradley Headstone is stalking Eugene Wrayburn by the river — it's one of the most frightening things in English Victorian fiction.
The light dying, the river darkening — and then Dickens writes:
'the red had the appearance of fading out of it and mounting up to Heaven, as we say that blood, guiltily shed, does.'
'Guiltily shed' — that phrase does not belong to the murderer alone; it belongs to every social arrangement that produced Bradley Headstone's rage.
The landscape is a conscience.
And it's precisely that moral atmosphere — blood mounting to heaven, dust-heaps, bodies in the river — that makes Bella's arc feel earned rather than merely sentimental.
She is changing inside a novel that takes the consequences of moral failure absolutely seriously.
The satire of the charity patrons is part of that same moral seriousness — Mr Boffin cataloguing the absurdity of philanthropic vanity.
He lists them with magnificent contempt:
'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses — what does it all mean?'
The accumulation is Dickens at his most Rabelaisian — the words multiply until they expose their own emptiness.
Bella observes all of this — the philanthropy pantomime, the Boffin household's sudden wealth-sickness — and it shapes her.
What's remarkable in all three of your readings is how interconnected Bella's arc is with the novel's larger moral geography.
She doesn't change in isolation — she changes inside a world where the river consumes, where charity is often vanity, where even a rooftop garden is a kind of paradise under siege.
In our next segment, we'll look more closely at what exactly Bella becomes — and whether Dickens fully trusts his own heroine.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Reading the Rhythms: Dickens's Prose as Musical Performance

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens's great late novel apart — lovingly — to see how it works.
Today's segment is about something I find endlessly fascinating: the sheer musical quality of Dickens's prose.
The rhythms, the comic timing, the way a sentence can land like a punchline or a blow — sometimes both at once.
I'm joined today by three brilliant readers of this novel.
Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who is drawn, almost compulsively, to the architecture of how great sentences are built.
James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — he keeps us honest about what Dickens's world actually looked like on the ground.
And Caroline Woodcourt has been reading this novel since she was a teenager, and nobody — nobody — reads a passage aloud quite like she does.
Caroline, I want to start with you, because today's passages are yours — and they are a masterclass in Dickensian comic rhythm.
Where do you want to begin?
I want to start with the Lammles, because that passage is so brief — barely three lines — and yet it is doing so much.
Dickens sets up this picture of conjugal bliss — the delightful interchanges, the loving looks — and you can feel him almost relishing the irony.
And then comes the turn, and it's so perfectly timed that it functions like a comic drumroll landing on the wrong beat.
Listen to what he actually writes:
'How delightful those interchanges, and the looks accompanying them! Now, if the skeleton up-stairs had taken that opportunity, for instance, of calling out — Here I am, suffocating in the closet!'
That 'for instance' is the thing that kills me.
It's so casual, as if Dickens is musing aloud, as if the skeleton's eruption is just one option among many he's idly considering.
The colloquial ease of it — that 'for instance' — is what makes the grotesque image land as comedy rather than horror.
Yes — and I'd call that a kind of deliberate bathos, but bathos wielded with complete precision.
The exclamation mark after 'How delightful those interchanges' is doing sarcastic work, of course — that's the mock-enthusiastic register Dickens slips in and out of like a coat.
But then structurally, the sentence pivots on 'Now, if' — which is the narrator stepping forward, almost nudging us.
There's a brilliant architectural move at work: the narrator performs the same kind of social performance as the Lammles — all delightful surface — and then deliberately punctures it.
The form enacts the content — a facade with a skeleton behind it.
I find myself less amused by the skeleton — though I grant the wit is superb — and more struck by the particular social institution the Lammles represent.
The 'fraud' in that marriage is not metaphorical — it is legally and financially precise.
Each deceived the other about their fortune before they married, and mid-Victorian law offered essentially no remedy once that deceit was discovered within marriage.
So when Dickens puts the skeleton in the closet, he is being quite literal about the machinery of that trap — and the comedy has a genuinely merciless edge.
That merciless edge is exactly what I feel in the Deputy Lock passage — but the target is different, and the comedy is darker, even if it's dressed up as farce.
Poor Betty Higden needs help, and this man pockets his coins one by one while performing his own virtue to her face.
And Dickens captures the performance in a single stage direction that is almost unbearable:

'I'm a man as earns his living by the sweat of his brow' — here he drew his sleeve across his forehead, as if this particular portion of his humble gains were the result of sheer hard labour and virtuous industry.
'As if.' Those two words carry the whole accusation.
Dickens doesn't say the man is a hypocrite — he shows you the gesture and then steps back with that devastating 'as if.'
And then: 'Go where you like.' A dismissal wrapped in fake magnanimity.
The grammar is doing something very clever there — that parenthetical stage direction interrupts the Deputy's own speech mid-sentence.
So we hear his words, then see the gesture, then hear the conclusion — and in that three-beat structure the gap between word and act is made visible.
It's a formally perfect sentence of exposure — Dickens uses the architecture of reported speech to catch the man in the act of lying.
A novelist can do that — inhabit the gap between what someone says and what they do — in a way that almost no other form can.
And the institutional context here is, if anything, grimmer than the Lammle scene.
The Deputy Lock is a petty official — one of those figures who exist at the threshold between the destitute and the system supposedly designed to help them.
Betty Higden's terror of the workhouse runs all through this novel, and Dickens is furious about it in a way he rarely lets show so plainly.
The comedy of that sleeve-wipe is Dickens deploying absurdity as a controlled weapon — because to describe this without the wit would be simply unbearable.
Which brings me to the passage I find almost purely joyful — Sloppy and Wegg.
Because there the darkness lifts completely, and Dickens lets himself be openly, childishly delighted by the rightness of it.
Wegg has schemed throughout the novel, and his ending is not a trial or a moral speech — it is a scavenger's cart.
The passage needs to be heard in full — let me read it:
'Sloppy lightly trotted out with him and trotted down the staircase, Mr Venus attending to open the street door.'

'Mr Sloppy's instructions had been to deposit his burden in the road; but, a scavenger's cart happening to stand unattended at the corner, with its little ladder planted against the wheel, Mr S. found it impossible to resist the temptation of shooting Mr Silas Wegg into the cart's contents.'
'A somewhat difficult feat, achieved with great dexterity, and with a prodigious splash.'
'A prodigious splash.' That full stop after 'splash' is one of the great full stops in English comic prose.
The formal control in that final sentence is astonishing — three short clauses, each with its own weight, building to maximum bathos.
'A somewhat difficult feat' — that 'somewhat' is doing everything, signalling modesty about an act of comic violence.
'Achieved with great dexterity' — and there we get the mock-heroic elevation, Sloppy momentarily cast as an athlete or a craftsman.
And then 'with a prodigious splash' — the tricolon resolves into pure onomatopoeic squalor.
The word 'prodigious' is itself comically oversized for a splash — which is exactly the point.
Notice also the justice being administered here — and by whom.
Sloppy is not a gentleman, not a magistrate, not any figure of official authority — he is a foundling who grew up on the dust mounds.
And he deposits Wegg back into the dust with what Dickens describes as great dexterity — as if this is his natural métier, his proper genius.
The novel is full of ironic reversals, but this one has a particular symbolic neatness that I think Dickens must have planned from the beginning.
And before we finish with these passages, I want to note the threat that comes just before all of this — from the Secretary to Wegg.
Because it's delivered with such cold precision that it reads almost like verse:
'Be careful what insolent liberties you take in that gentleman's presence, or I will throw you after it.'
'I will throw you after it.' Not 'I may,' not 'you risk being thrown' — 'I will.'
The future indicative, completely flat, completely certain.
It's the most thrillingly direct sentence in a chapter full of beautiful indirection.
It's a sentence that trusts the reader entirely — no explanation, no elaboration, no sentiment.
Dickens at his most controlled is Dickens at his most terrifying — because you realize the exuberance elsewhere is a choice, not an inability to stop.
He can pull the register down to ice, and then the warmth everywhere else feels earned rather than merely habitual.
That image — warmth that is earned rather than habitual — feels like a perfect place to pause on this segment.
What we've seen in all four of these passages is a writer who never lets the prose coast — who understands that rhythm, grammar, and register are moral instruments as much as aesthetic ones.
Thank you, Caroline, Eleanor, and James — that was a genuine pleasure.
Coming up next, we turn our attention to the social institutions at the heart of this novel — and what they tell us about power, money, and the people who fall between the cracks.

segments.title: Closing: The Redemption We Earn—Love, Complicity, and Dickens's Final Word

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracing the novel's great currents — money, identity, the river itself.
Now, in closing, I want us to ask the hardest question: what does Dickens actually believe about redemption?
Is it earned? Is it given freely? And who, in the end, is denied it entirely?
Eleanor, you've been sitting with Bradley Headstone's final chapters, and I suspect you have something urgent to say.
Urgent is exactly right, because what Dickens does with Bradley in those final pages is structurally extraordinary.
Most novelists, when they condemn a character, simply withdraw the light from them.
Dickens does something far more unsettling — he keeps the camera absolutely steady on Bradley's disintegration.
There's this passage where he sits through the night, rigid and consumed, and the prose becomes almost geological in its patience.

"Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair degenerating."
That word — degenerating — is doing so much work.
It's not just physical decay. It's ontological collapse — the self literally coming apart at the seams.
And yet Dickens denies Bradley even the dignity of remorse, which is a theological and a legal distinction worth pausing on.
In Victorian jurisprudence, remorse was one of the few avenues toward mitigation — toward any narrative of rehabilitation.
Dickens closes that door deliberately, and what replaces it is something he describes with chilling precision.
"He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently."
More efficiently — that is the knife in the sentence.
The criminal mind, lacking conscience, optimises. It replays the crime not in horror but in a kind of grim professional review.
And Dickens insists this compulsive perfectionism is itself a punishment — heavier, he suggests, than any remorse could be.
What strikes me, reading those two passages together, is how merciless Dickens is — and how honest that mercilessness is.
We talk about Dickens as a sentimental writer, and sometimes he earns that charge.
But here, with Bradley, there is no softening. There is no deathbed epiphany.
The ashes spread. The hair degenerates. And he earns every syllable of it.
But then — and this is where the novel's moral geography becomes so intricate — you put that against Bella's story.
And Lizzie's account of the children ruined by drink — children without even a cradle to begin from — reminds you how much of character in this novel is circumstance.
Lizzie says of this poor little creature: "This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley."
That parenthetical — if she ever had one — is almost unbearable. It's said almost in passing, and it annihilates you.
Caroline, yes — and that's precisely why the Boffins matter so much to the novel's argument about redemption.
Because if circumstance can damn — if a child without a cradle is already half-lost — then what rescues anyone?
Dickens's answer, I think, is disinterested goodness — and he makes it concrete through Boffin.
When John Harmon confronts Wegg, he spells out exactly what he owes, and the language strains under the weight of genuine gratitude.
"I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin."
That parenthesis — there are no words to satisfy me — is Dickens acknowledging the limits of his own instrument.
The novelist says: language fails here. And that failure is the sincerest tribute he can pay.
What I find remarkable from a historical standpoint is how deliberately Dickens separates moral worth from legal title.
Harmon technically inherits by law. But Dickens insists the real transaction is the Boffins' gift — freely given, unconditional.
The mounds — that pile of Victorian industrial waste — are redeemed by being passed through the hands of people who handle them with generosity.
That's a radical moral proposition, even now. Money is not self-justifying; it requires ethical stewardship to become legitimate.
And yet Dickens never lets the optimism become cheap. The novel ends with survivors — not triumphants.
Lizzie has lost Eugene to near-death and to the river. Bella has had to become someone she wasn't born being.
Even the Boffins absorb the cruelty of Wegg's scheming and Harmon's long deception without being broken by it.
Redemption in this novel is always earned through endurance and through love — and it costs something real.
What a note to close on — redemption earned through endurance, not granted by magic or sentiment.
Eleanor, James, Caroline — you've made this novel feel as necessary and as alive as anything written in the last year. Thank you.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel about what the river gives back — and what it keeps.
Dickens asks, finally, whether any of us can be made clean by love and time and the choices we make under pressure.
His answer — complicated, merciful, and unsparing in equal measure — is what makes this the great novel it is.
Thank you for listening to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked. We'll see you next time.

      now appeared to be less of a minion and more of a worm than had been
      previously supposed. That, he considered it plain that such price was
      stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, ‘Halves!’

      he had a plan of action to recommend, with a conditional clause. That, the
      plan of action was that they should lie by with patience; that, they
      should allow the Mounds to be gradually levelled and cleared away, while
      retaining to themselves their present opportunity of watching the process—which
      would be, he conceived, to put the trouble and cost of daily digging and
      delving upon somebody else, while they might nightly turn such complete
      disturbance of the dust to the account of their own private investigations—and
      that, when the Mounds were gone, and they had worked those chances for
      their own joint benefit solely, they should then, and not before, explode
      on the minion and worm. But here came the conditional clause, and to this
      he entreated the special attention of his comrade, brother, and partner.

      that property which was now to be regarded as their own property. When he,
      Mr Wegg, had seen the minion surreptitiously making off with that bottle,
      and its precious contents unknown, he had looked upon him in the light of
      a mere robber, and, as such, would have despoiled him of his ill-gotten
      gain, but for the judicious interference of his comrade, brother, and
      partner. Therefore, the conditional clause he proposed was, that, if the
      minion should return in his late sneaking manner, and if, being closely
      watched, he should be found to possess himself of anything, no matter
      what, the sharp sword impending over his head should be instantly shown
      him, he should be strictly examined as to what he knew or suspected,
      should be severely handled by them his masters, and should be kept in a
      state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should
      see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his
      possessions. If, said Mr Wegg by way of peroration, he had erred in saying
      only ‘Halves!’ he trusted to his comrade, brother, and partner not to
      hesitate to set him right, and to reprove his weakness. It might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths. On those points

      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on

      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally

These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?

c65:p104.text:
Not one other word did Bradley utter all that night. Not once did he
      change his attitude, or loosen his hold upon his wrist. Rigid before the
      fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with
      the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more
      haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being
      overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair
      degenerating.
c65:p104.summary: Bradley sits all night in rigid despair, his face aging, whitening, and degenerating as if being consumed by internal fire while Riderhood maintains his vigilance.
c65:p104.best_quote: Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair degenerating.

c57:p53.text:
Now, too, was he cursed with a state of mind more wearing and more
      wearisome than remorse. He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold
      that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing
      the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently. In the defensive
      declarations and pretended confessions of murderers, the pursuing shadow
      of this torture may be traced through every lie they tell. If I had done
      it as alleged, is it conceivable that I would have made this and this
      mistake? If I had done it as alleged, should I have left that unguarded
      place which that false and wicked witness against me so infamously deposed
      to? The state of that wretch who continually finds the weak spots in his
      own crime, and strives to strengthen them when it is unchangeable, is a
      state that aggravates the offence by doing the deed a thousand times
      instead of once; but it is a state, too, that tauntingly visits the
      offence upon a sullen unrepentant nature with its heaviest punishment
      every time.
c57:p53.summary: The narrator explores the psychological torment of murderers without remorse: they are compelled to endlessly re-enact and mentally perfect their crime, creating a torture worse than remorse itself.
c57:p53.best_quote: He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently.

c18:p149.text:
‘The child’s father is employed by the house that employs me; that’s how I
      came to know it, Charley. The father is like his own father, a weak
      wretched trembling creature, falling to pieces, never sober. But a good
      workman too, at the work he does. The mother is dead. This poor ailing
      little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people
      from her cradle—if she ever had one, Charley.’
c18:p149.summary: Lizzie explains that Bella's father is employed by her employer and shares his father's weakness for drink; her mother is dead, and the child is surrounded by alcoholics and degradation.
c18:p149.best_quote: This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle—if she ever had one, Charley.

c64:p101.text:
‘Now, scoundrel,’ he pursued, ‘I am going to finish. You supposed me just
      now, to be the possessor of my father’s property.—So I am. But
      through any act of my father’s, or by any right I have? No. Through the
      munificence of Mr Boffin. The conditions that he made with me, before
      parting with the secret of the Dutch bottle, were, that I should take the
      fortune, and that he should take his Mound and no more. I owe everything I
      possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness,
      goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin. And
      when, knowing what I knew, I saw such a mud-worm as you presume to rise in
      this house against this noble soul, the wonder is,’ added John Harmon
      through his clenched teeth, and with a very ugly turn indeed on Wegg’s
      cravat, ‘that I didn’t try to twist your head off, and fling  that  out of
      window! So. That’s the last short speech, do you understand?’
c64:p101.summary: Harmon explains that he owes his fortune entirely to Boffin's generosity, and his fury at Wegg's presumption against such a noble soul.
c64:p101.best_quote: I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin.
